The negative AI jobs outcome just continues to not be happening as some predicted. A large portion of enterprises I talk with -across industries- are still hiring, just with a tilt in the kind of roles they’re going after.

They’re finding that AI is letting them do more, and Jevons paradox is actually playing out. They’re hiring engineers to go after problems they couldn’t tackle before. They’re hiring in sales because they can go deeper in client relationships now with the help of AI. They’re hiring in internal FDEs to help them deploy AI. And so on.

Anyone using AI merely to cut costs eventually just gets outcompeted by companies that use AI to better serve their customers and drive more breakthroughs in their business. 

Could this trend change at some point? Sure. But for now this appears to be the trajectory we’re on.

"Sample-Efficient Learning from Agent Experience"

Agents can learn from trial and error in context, but forget once the context is gone. 

This paper propose something called Experience Distillation. So you let an experience-conditioned teacher look at old agent rollouts, ask it for the next decision at real history points, then train the student to make those decisions without the experience context.

No extra environment rollouts and no long synthetic trajectories needed, while also keeping up to 93.4% of ICL gains. It also matches RL baselines with at least 9.6x fewer environment samples.

tweets.text:
China today made its biggest move deep in the AI stack: it began producing its own chip-making machine and homegrown ASML.

Yuliangsheng, tied to Huawei and SiCarrier, is now mass-producing immersion DUV lithography machines, the tools that make 7nm chips. their first deliveries are this year, to SMIC, the makers of Huawei’s Ascend chips, Hua Hong and CXMT, memory manufacturers.

The China AI compute supply chain can be thought of as ASML : Yuliangsheng -> TSMC : SMIC -> Nvidia : Huawei.

SMIC makes 7nm node chips using immersion DUV systems on ASML tools bought before the various sanctions. If the current MATCH Act passes, they can’t even be serviced. China desperately needs Yuliangsheng to ramp capacity to increase the domestic compute production, even on yesteryears nodes.

The current machines are equivalents of ASML NXT:1980Di, a 28nm tool that reaches 7nm with multi-patterning, which is 10-15yrs behind frontier. For comparison, the new Vera Rubins are on an EUV 3nm node. And China’s still ramping capacity, projecting 20 machines in 2027 vs ~130 DUV/yr and ~45 EUV/yr from ASML.

This also has tons of caveats. They rely on critical parts from Japan. New scanners need 12-18mos of tuning per fab. Yields take a long long time to get right. But China tends to be quite good at manufacturing at scale.

Even though they’re far behind on frontier tech, this is a significant milestone to China owning its homegrown AI supply chain. Maybe not in 5yrs, but maybe 10, they’re going to mass produce compute that could be quite threatening. With largely better manufacturing abilities and fewer regulatory hurdles to deploy data centers at scale with ample power, this poses a real risk to the balance of global compute.
🥸 https://t.co/Vc1ggIUzX0
